passages.happening: Solomon declares, “The LORD has said that He would dwell in the thick cloud” (verse 1), and he says to God that he has built an exalted house, ‘a place for You to dwell forever’ (verse 2). He turns and speaks to the assembly (verse 3). God brought Israel out of Egypt and chose no city until he chose Jerusalem, and chose David (verses 4-6). David had it in his heart to build, and God told him his son would build instead (verses 7-9). ‘Now the LORD has fulfilled the word that He spoke’ (verse 10), and the ark is in its place (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The glory cloud has just filled the house, and Solomon answers with words. His speech and prayer say what the temple means: not a home that confines God, but a place toward which Israel can turn in every kind of trouble and be heard. The prayer works almost as a charter for the rest of 2 Chronicles. Again and again later kings will face defeat, drought, invasion and exile, and the question will be whether they turn and pray as Solomon asked. God answers in chapter 7.

The language of God's Name dwelling in the temple comes from Deuteronomy, which speaks of the place the LORD will choose for his Name. In the ancient world a name stood for a person's reputation, authority and presence. To say God's Name is in the temple is to say he is truly present and can be called on there, while he himself dwells in heaven.
passages.later: Deuteronomy had spoken of ‘the place the LORD your God will choose from among all your tribes to establish as a dwelling for His Name’ (Deuteronomy 12:5).
passages.asks: Solomon's first words were about God keeping his word to David. Ask which of God's promises you have seen kept. And ask whether you speak of them to others as Solomon did to the assembly.

passages.t: The prayer: hear from heaven, and forgive
passages.happening:
Solomon stands on a bronze platform in the courtyard, kneels before the whole assembly and spreads his hands toward heaven (verse 13). “O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven or on earth, keeping Your covenant of loving devotion with Your servants who walk before You with all their hearts” (verse 14). He asks God to keep his promise to David (verses 15-17), and then: ‘But will God indeed dwell with man upon the earth? Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built’ (verse 18).

He asks God to hear what is prayed toward this place: ‘May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place. May You hear and forgive’ (verse 21). Then come seven cases: a disputed oath, defeat in battle, drought, famine and plague, the foreigner who comes ‘because of Your great name’ (verse 32), war, and captivity. Last of all, when Israel sins, ‘for there is no one who does not sin’ (verse 36), and is carried captive, and repents in the land of the captors and prays toward the land and the city and the house, ‘May You forgive Your people who sinned against You’ (verse 39).

The prayer ends with a psalm: ‘Now therefore, arise, O LORD God, and enter Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might’ (verse 41), and ‘O LORD God, do not reject Your anointed one. Remember Your loving devotion to Your servant David’ (verse 42).
passages.hearers:
The prayer is found almost word for word in 1 Kings 8. The Chronicler adds the bronze platform, about seven and a half feet square and four and a half high, on which Solomon stood and knelt. He changes the ending: Kings closes with God's choice of Israel at the exodus through Moses, and Chronicles with lines from Psalm 132, a psalm about David's vow to find a resting place for the ark. The emphasis falls on David, the ark and the temple.

Standing, then kneeling, with open hands lifted, was the common posture of prayer in the ancient world. A king kneeling in public was a statement: Israel's king was not divine and was himself a petitioner. The oath at the altar in verse 22 reflects an old legal practice: where evidence was lacking, a person could swear before the altar and trust God to judge.

Three words run through the prayer. Hear, shama, comes twelve times; in Hebrew hearing often means hearing and acting. Forgive, salach, has only God as its subject in the Old Testament. Turn, shuv, is the Old Testament's main word for repentance. Anointed one, mashiach, in verse 42 means Solomon, the king of David's line; from it comes the word Messiah.

For the Chronicler's readers the petition about exile was not hypothetical. Their parents and grandparents had been carried to Babylon, and many had prayed toward a ruined Jerusalem. The later Jewish practice of praying toward Jerusalem grows from this prayer.
passages.later: In Babylon, Daniel ‘went into his house, where the windows of his upper room opened toward Jerusalem, and three times a day he got down on his knees, prayed, and gave thanks to his God’ (Daniel 6:10). The psalm says, ‘Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength’ (Psalm 132:8).
passages.hard:
Did Israel believe God actually lived in the temple?

Solomon says both that he has built God a place to dwell forever (verse 2) and that heaven itself cannot contain God (verse 18), and the prayer asks God again and again to hear from heaven, his dwelling place. Some readers see a contradiction, or a change from an older belief that God lived in the temple to a later belief that he lived in heaven.

Most interpreters see the tension as deliberate. The Old Testament holds together God's being above and beyond all creation and his being truly present in particular places and ways. The temple was a real meeting place where God's Name dwelt and his glory could be seen, but it was never his container. Some scholars trace a development in Israel's thought, linked with Deuteronomy's language of the Name; others argue that both ideas were there from the beginning. Either way, the prayer insists on both: God is here, and God is not confined here. The prophets would later warn that treating the temple as a guarantee of safety was a false trust.
passages.asks: Solomon prayed for the stranger who would come from far away, and for sinners in a foreign land, because there is no one who does not sin. Ask whether your prayers make room for people outside your own circle. And ask what you would pray if you were the one far from home.
